title: Deconstruction and Derrida
welcome_lead: Jacques Derrida arrives — and certainty unravels. Walk the deconstructive corridor.
meta_desc: Deconstruction and Derrida at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You have followed Derrida's pen and watched stable oppositions disclose their dependence on what they exclude.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Derrida coined différance in 1968 to capture both difference (signs gain meaning from others) and deferral (meaning never fully arrives).

The word is pronounced like différence — the change is visible in writing, audible only to the reader.
In Of Grammatology (1967) Derrida reads Rousseau's account of writing as supplement to speech and shows the 'supplement' is in fact prior — speech depends on the very thing it supposedly precedes.
Paul de Man, Geoffrey Hartman, J. Hillis Miller and Harold Bloom — the Yale School — brought deconstruction into English departments, applying it to Romantic poetry and beyond.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a theme and a symbol?
options: A theme is the title of the book.
Gothic refers to medieval architecture, not literature.
A theme is an abstract idea or concern the text explores (e.g. mortality); a symbol is a concrete image that stands for something else (e.g. a skull).
Themes are just symbols repeated through the book.

mcqs.q: What defines epic poetry as a genre?
options: A theme is the title of the book.
Long narrative poems on heroic subjects, in elevated style, often invoking a muse, in medias res openings, and treating events of national or cosmic significance.
Epic means any poem that is very long.
Epic means any story with a battle in it.

mcqs.q: What are conventions of the Gothic genre?
options: Gothic just means scary stories with vampires and ghosts.
Gothic refers to medieval architecture, not literature.
Epic means any story with a battle in it.
Settings of ruin and decay, supernatural or psychological terror, transgression of boundaries, the sublime, doubled or haunted protagonists, and atmospheric excess.
